figures.title: The fat family tree: the map of this lesson

segments.text: Here is the map of where this lesson is heading. We'll build up to each branch, starting from single atoms.
Every fat gives 9 calories per gram; protein and carbs give 4.
Saturated fats have no double bonds; that's Figure 3. Monounsaturated fats have one double bond; that's Figure 5.
Polyunsaturated fats have two or more, and they include the omega-3 and omega-6 families, in Figures 5 and 6.
Trans fats are mostly made from unsaturated oils by partial hydrogenation. That's the dashed arrow, and we'll cover it in Figures 3 and 7.

A bond is the attraction that holds two atoms together in a molecule. In the fats we're looking at, it's mostly carbon sharing electrons with hydrogen or with another carbon, and that sharing is what builds the chains.
segments.cue: Meet the atoms, panel A: C and H share one pair of electrons (blue dots)

segments.text: Atoms have electrons in shells around them, and atoms are happiest when their outer shell is full. A bond is when two atoms share a pair of those outer electrons so each one gets to count them.
segments.cue: Panel A again: the shared pair

segments.text: One shared pair is a single bond, which lets the atoms spin freely around each other. Two shared pairs is a double bond, which is shorter, stronger, and locks the atoms in place so they can't rotate.
segments.cue: Panel B: single bond rotates, double bond is locked

segments.text: That's the whole trick behind saturated versus unsaturated fat: saturated chains are all single bonds, so they lie straight and pack tight. Unsaturated ones have double bonds that put a kink in the chain, and that's what keeps oils liquid.
segments.cue: Panel C: straight saturated chain vs kinked cis chain

segments.text: One footnote: the kink comes from cis double bonds; trans double bonds stay nearly straight. We'll see that in Figure 3.
Now the triglyceride image. Almost every fat you eat, and the fat stored in your body, is one kind of molecule: a triglyceride.
The purple box on the left is the glycerol backbone, three carbons. Hanging off it are three fatty acids.

Each fatty acid starts with an acid head, the end with the red oxygens. On its own it's a carboxyl group, COOH, and it reacts with one of glycerol's OH groups, giving off water, to make an ester link: the red bar.
segments.cue: Red oxygens and red ester bar

segments.text: The long part sticking out to the right is the carbon tail: a zigzag of carbons numbered from the head, C1, out to the far end, the omega end.
Only three elements: carbon makes 4 bonds, oxygen 2, and hydrogen 1. Hydrogens are hidden here to keep it clean.
In the tails, one line between carbons is a single bond; the orange pair with two lines is a C=C double bond. A double-bonded carbon has room for fewer hydrogens.
The top chain has no double bonds, the middle one has one, and the bottom one has two.
Now the last image, fat versus oil. On the left is tristearin, three straight saturated chains; it melts at about 72 °C, so it's solid.
On the right is triolein, three kinked chains with one cis double bond each; it melts at about 5 °C, so it's liquid.
Same kind of molecule, same elements: C, H and O. The oil just has six fewer hydrogens because of its three double bonds.

'Fat' or 'oil' only tells you whether it's solid or liquid at room temperature, about 20 to 25 °C. Real fats are mixes: coconut oil is mostly saturated and melts around 24 °C, so it's solid in a cool kitchen and liquid in a warm one.
We'll see why shape matters in Figure 4. And trans fats, which we meet in Figure 3, are mostly man-made.
Same 18 carbons, three ways, and this time the small white hydrogens are shown.
Top: stearic acid, saturated. No double bonds, so every tail carbon holds as many hydrogens as it can, two each and three on the end, and the zigzag runs straight. It melts at about 69 °C.
Middle: oleic acid. Between C9 and C10 there's an orange double bond, and two hydrogens are gone; that's what 'unsaturated' means.
The two hydrogens left on that bond sit on the same side, which is called cis, and that bends the chain. It melts at about 13 °C.
Bottom: elaidic acid, trans. Same double bond in the same place, but the hydrogens sit on opposite sides, so the chain stays nearly straight and melts at about 45 °C.
So trans fat behaves much like saturated fat. Plant oils and most natural fats are cis.

Most trans fat in food was man-made, by partial hydrogenation of vegetable oil, which we'll see in Figure 7. Small natural amounts come from ruminant animals, cows, sheep and goats, so dairy, beef and lamb contain a little; the main one is vaccenic acid.
In the pink box: saturated fat is part of the structure of your cell membranes and a dense backup fuel stored in fat tissue.
Your liver can build cholesterol from fat breakdown products, and cholesterol is the raw material for steroid hormones. So the hormones come from cholesterol, not from saturated fat directly.
But eating a lot of saturated fat raises LDL, the 'bad' cholesterol.
Trans fat: your body doesn't handle the straight trans shape like natural unsaturated fat; it packs into cell membranes much like saturated fat.
Trans fat raises LDL, the 'bad' cholesterol, and lowers HDL, the 'good' one, and it is strongly linked to heart disease. That's why industrial trans fat is now mostly banned in the US.
Ruminant trans fat is eaten in much smaller amounts. At normal intakes the evidence of harm is weaker, but in high-dose trials it raises LDL too.

figures.title: Why some fats are solid and some oils are liquid

segments.text: This is the space-filling style: every atom at its true size, so each fatty acid looks like a solid rod.
On the left, four straight saturated chains stack tightly, like pencils in a box. They grip each other, so it takes more heat to melt them: about 69 °C for stearic acid.
That's why butter, lard and cocoa butter are solid at room temperature.
In the middle, trans chains are almost straight, so they pack almost as tightly and melt at about 45 °C. That's why partially hydrogenated oil turned solid.
On the right, the cis kinks keep oleic chains apart and leave gaps, so they slide past each other and melt at about 13 °C. That's why olive and canola oil are liquid.
In real fats these chains sit on triglycerides, like in Figure 2, and the same rule holds.
Unsaturated fats are grouped by how many double bonds they have.
Top: oleic acid, monounsaturated, 'mono' meaning one: a single cis double bond at C9. It's the main fat in olive oil.
Bottom: linoleic acid, polyunsaturated, 'poly' meaning many, with two cis double bonds at C9 and C12. It's in sunflower, corn and other seed oils.
Each extra kink lowers the melting point again: about 13 °C for oleic, about minus 5 °C for linoleic.
In the pink box: monounsaturated fat, mostly oleic acid, is the main fat in your stored body fat, your energy reserve. It helps keep cell membranes flexible.
Diets that swap saturated fat for monounsaturated fat are linked to better cholesterol numbers, with lower LDL and a better LDL-to-HDL balance.
All polyunsaturated fats: the parent omega-3 and omega-6 are essential, so your body can't make them and they must come from food. It uses them to build signaling molecules called eicosanoids.

figures.title: Omega-3 vs omega-6: count from the tail

segments.text: Now count from the tail. Omega 1 is the last carbon.
On top is ALA, the plant omega-3 in flax, chia and walnuts. It has three cis double bonds, and the first one starts at omega 3, so it's an omega-3.
Below is linoleic acid, the main omega-6 in seed oils like sunflower and corn oil. It has two double bonds, and the first starts at omega 6, so it's an omega-6.
Omega-3: its signals tend to calm inflammation, and DHA is a major building block of your brain and the retina of your eye.
Plant ALA converts only poorly into EPA and DHA, so fish or algae are the direct sources.
Omega-6: through arachidonic acid it makes the signals for immune responses, inflammation and blood clotting. Those are useful jobs.
But too much omega-6 compared with omega-3 may tip the balance toward inflammation.

figures.title: Hydrogenation: how oils become solid fats

segments.text: This is how factories turn liquid oil into solid fat: they add hydrogen gas with a nickel catalyst and heat.
Full hydrogenation, at the bottom, removes every double bond and gives saturated fat.
Partial hydrogenation, in the middle, stops partway: some double bonds remain and some flip from cis to trans.
That's where most trans fat in food came from, the man-made trans fat from Figure 3. Industrial trans fat is banned in the US and limited in the EU.
Top: melting points of the pure fatty acids. The dashed line is room temperature.
Anything above it, like stearic and elaidic acid, is solid in your kitchen; anything below, like oleic, linoleic and ALA, is liquid.
Straighter chains melt higher, every cis kink lowers the melting point, and longer chains melt higher.
Bottom: the same idea inside you. Stored body fat is mostly triglycerides, and most of their fatty acids are unsaturated, with oleic acid the most common.
So it stays soft at body temperature, about 37 °C. Fat just under the cooler skin is firmer, and fat deeper in is softer.

You'll sometimes hear that the body keeps its outer fat layers more unsaturated so they don't harden. That's well shown in pigs and other animals, but the evidence in humans is weaker, so treat it as a maybe.
That completes the family tree from Figure 1: saturated, mono, poly with the omegas, and trans. The quiz is below.
